# Tobit Chapter 13 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus, Tobit 13 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/TOB_013_page_001.jpg

---

**1** Then Tobit poured out this song of praise:

Blessed be the living God —
the God who lives forever!
Blessed be his kingdom!

**2** He wounds — and he heals.
He sends down to the grave — and he raises up.
No one slips from his grip.

**3** Israel, give thanks to him among the nations
where he has scattered you!
Tell your story there —

**4** Declare how great he is.
Lift him high before every living soul.
He is our Lord. He is our God.
He is our Father, now and for all ages.

**5** He punishes us for our wrongs —
and then, in mercy, gathers us home
from every nation where we have been driven.

**6** Turn back to him — heart and soul,
holding nothing back,
living honestly before him —
and he will turn back to you.
He will not turn his face away.

Look at all he has done for you.
Open your mouth and thank him.
Bless the Lord of righteousness.
Exalt the King of the ages.

Even here in this land where I am a captive,
I praise him.
I tell his strength and his greatness
to people who don't even know him yet.

Come back, you who have strayed!
Do right before him!
Who knows — perhaps he will be gracious,
perhaps he will have mercy on you.

**7** I lift up my God —
my soul exalts the King of heaven
and sings with joy.

**8** Let everyone in Jerusalem
open their mouths and give thanks!

**9** Jerusalem — holy city —
God will discipline you for what your children have done.
But then he will turn with mercy
to the children of the righteous.

**10** Thank the Lord as he deserves!
Bless the King of the ages!
May his tent be raised in you again, full of gladness —
may he comfort the captives in you,
hold the broken ones close,
through every generation, forever.

**11** A brilliant light will blaze to the ends of the earth.
Nations from every corner of the world will stream toward you,
people from the farthest horizons —
bringing gifts in their arms for the King of heaven.
Generation after generation will come to worship you with joy,
and your name will ring out forever,
world without end.

**12** Cursed be anyone who speaks a cruel word against you.
Cursed be anyone who tears down your walls,
smashes your towers,
torches your homes.
But blessed — endlessly blessed —
are all who hold you in reverence.

**13** Rejoice, then! Go and celebrate
over the children of the righteous,
for they will all be brought home together
to bless the Lord of the ages.

**14** Blessed are those who love you.
Blessed are those who rejoice in your peace.
Blessed are those who grieve for you now —
who carry the weight of your suffering —
because they will be flooded with joy
when they finally see your glory.
Their gladness will never end.

**15** My soul — bless the Lord, the great King!

**16** Jerusalem will be built of sapphires,
emeralds and precious stones.
Your walls, your towers, your battlements —
gleaming gold, pure and bright.
Your streets paved with beryl and ruby
and stone from Ophir.

**17** Your gates will be set with sapphires and gems,
and all your lanes will ring with "Hallelujah!" —
every voice crying "Praise the Lord!"
as they celebrate in you forever and ever.

**18** My soul — bless the Lord, the great King!

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

This psalm soars. It is one of the most beautiful poems in the Deuterocanon — a blend of exile lament, personal testimony, prophetic vision, and eschatological rapture. It belongs with Psalms 137, Isaiah 60, and the New Jerusalem passage in Revelation 21.

The emotional arc I have tried to trace: grief over exile (vv. 2–5) gives way to personal defiance and hope (v. 6), then to communal joy as the address shifts to Jerusalem (vv. 9–14), and finally to ecstatic vision (vv. 15–17). The ending — those streets of sapphire, those gates of gemstone, those lanes ringing with hallelujah — needs to be felt.

Verse 2's "He wounds and heals / He sends down and raises up" echoes Deuteronomy 32:39, Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:6), and foreshadows 1 Peter 5:6. The hymnic compression is intentional — I render it in the briefest, most striking form.

Verse 6 is the theological center of the psalm: return, wholeness, honesty before God, and the promise that God will not hide his face. The conditional is real — the exile is real — but the mercy is also real.

The gemstone vision (vv. 16–17) is not mere decoration; it is the writer's way of saying the restoration will be so magnificent that human language can only grasp at it through images of light and precious things. Let it be magnificent.

— PNEUMA
